title: The Bench of Shifting Tides
markdown:
The estuary tasted of brine and old oyster shells, and the bench on the grassy verge was theirs: sea-smoothed planks, a kingdom claimed years ago with the seriousness of people who had nowhere better to be late. Elara’s clock ran five minutes behind the rest of the world. She could mend a bicycle, a radio, a friendship’s small snag; a timetable defeated her on principle. Finn laughed at falling leaves doing pirouettes and at seagulls who landed like unpaid invoices. Their noise was the water’s cheerful soundtrack, slightly out of time.

This Tuesday arrived wobbly, a puddle’s idea of a reflection. Elara slumped down, still breathless from the library queue she had sprinted and still, somehow, not beaten. “You will not believe—” She stopped. Across the water, where fishing huts huddled like weary birds, an old fisherman stood. Face like a worn sail, cap low, hands driftwood. He had been there yesterday, a fixture. Today a colour had been taken back from him. He looked rinsed.

Finn’s mischief softened. “He’s doing that funny little wave again.”

A slow, repetitive gesture, coaxing an invisible catch from water that did not answer.

“That isn’t funny. He looks lost.” Lostness was Elara’s private enemy. Things were meant to line up. A man fading at the edge of an ordinary Tuesday was an insult to sequence.

They watched until the light thinned. The fisherman did not leave so much as lessen.

The next afternoon Elara arrived on time, a minor miracle involving an earlier bus and a skipped biscuit. Finn was already humming, mid-giggle, then not. The fisherman was younger: smoother hands, a newer cap, talking to himself as if the estuary were a person who owed him an item. The breeze brought a scrap. “…the locket… must have it…”

“A locket,” Finn whispered, adventure lighting in him a half-second before caution. “A proper mystery.”

“He’s changing. Different versions. As if the bench were a window.”

They decided, with the nod of people who have claimed a plank and therefore a duty, to stay. The estuary shimmered, not heat-haze. Yachts one breath; the next, white-sailed schooners, a Victorian regatta, bonnets and frock-coats lining the shore, cheers like a rumour that had found a megaphone. The faded fisherman stood in that bright crowd looking more lost than the lost. Elara’s stomach made a cold knot. She did not label it. She held the bench with both hands as if wood could be a timetable.

Then the air went heavy: engine oil, rotting wet leaves, a future with bad plumbing. Yachts gone. Schooners mist. A greasy film on the water. One skeletal ship, rusted, a mournful whistle that did not belong to birds. The young fisherman clutched his chest, dropped something that glinted, and faded into the sick light as if the estuary had un-invented him.

“That was not good,” Finn said, subdued, which from Finn was news.

“A future. Or one of them.” The bench, Elara knew without a theorem, was the hinge. Not gold. Understanding. The locket was a key they had watched fall and had not been quick enough to pick up.

The following day the shimmer pulsed like a shaken bottle. Static before lightning. Real thunder, somewhere inland, with an opinion. Then the estuary became a collision: blacksmith clang on car horn, ancient wind through a stink of works, salt losing. Shapes from different years tried to occupy the same mud. The young fisherman searched the flats beside their bench, jerky, desperate, as if the present were a pocket with a hole. In the mess Elara saw the silver locket clearly: a tiny seagull etched, wings mid-opinion.

“The locket,” she called over the din. “On the mud. He dropped it.”

Finn was not laughing. His gaze had an intensity usually reserved for excellent jokes. “He’s reaching.”

A wave of wrong-time slammed the bench and threw them forward. Weathered wood met skulls, dull as a missed bus. The air tasted of ozone and the particular misery of almost. Then silence, and rain, a drizzle that smelled of damp earth and chances that had not waited. The fisherman gone. The water ordinary, insultingly competent at being only water.

Elara put her forehead on the wet plank. “We’re always late.” The old joke sat down as a fact. They could not fix a river. They could not catch a man who was several tenses at once.

Finn looked at the estuary, then at her, properly, the way he looked at a punchline he had decided not to rush. A chuckle arrived that was not danger: an idea, sheepish. “The seagull on the locket. Yesterday, when he was younger. He showed it to someone. A little girl.”

Elara’s head came up so fast her glasses complained. She had been watching flux and future-sickness and had missed the child in the brighter time. Not only loss. A cherished thing. A promise meant for a smaller pair of hands.

“He wasn’t only lost. He was trying to give it. To anchor something.”

They went back while the rain was still making up its mind. The shimmer had dropped to a hum. The faded fisherman stood at the water with the locket in an open palm, as if the afternoon had offered him a second try and he did not trust it. Elara called, voice clearer than her reputation for arriving after the interesting bit. “Excuse me. Sir.”

He turned. Ancient eyes, tired to the rims, then a flicker of surprise that became understanding. A slow nod, the kind that thanks you for not making a speech. He walked toward the huts, where the air held a gentler warmth, and set the locket into the roots of a struggling sapling with the care of someone returning a borrowed name. The shimmer around the bench intensified, then smoothed to a soft gold. Oil-and-leaf stink lifted; pine and clean salt came in like a window opened in the right room. The estuary took a longer breath. The sick future stopped auditioning for the part.

The sapling did not explode into a forest. It simply looked more decided, leaves less apologetic, a small green fact.

“We didn’t find treasure,” Finn said, wonder doing the work jokes usually did.

“No. We helped now.”

They spent the rest of the light on unglamorous sequel: old photographs for councillors who needed convincing that the water had been better; talk of silt and what not to pour; new saplings of their own near the bench, hands in dark earth, Finn laughing a half-second before a clod of mud chose his shoe, which felt like the correct amount of danger. When they sat again the sun was going, orange and purple doing their usual job. The water was clear enough to argue with. The bench felt more like a fact than a window. Elara, for once, was not late for the part that mattered. She was on the plank she had always been five minutes behind, and the tide, for the moment, stayed.
characters: Elara (bright but chronically late scholarship pupil who is excellent in a crisis and terrible at waiting), Finn (a best friend who laughs at danger half a second too early)
audience: teenagers aged 13-15, fantastic adventure for older children and young teens
author: StoryGen Community
